summary:
Mission Control is a browser game that teaches people with no technical background how real space missions are planned, by letting them make the trade-offs themselves. Up to four players take the jobs of a real mission team: a Planner who controls the budget, a Scientist who chooses the instruments, a Designer who builds the spacecraft, and a Radio Operator who picks the ground stations. They negotiate over money, mass, power, data and time, hold a go/no-go poll, then launch.

The game never blocks a bad design. The mission flies in 3D, and if it fails, a debrief explains what went wrong, why, whose decision caused it and how to fix it, with a link to the NASA page that covers the idea.

It includes three mission types, three difficulty levels, a guided tutorial, solo and online play, and English and Arabic. It uses real NASA imagery and NASA learning resources.

It matters because space engineering is about teamwork and compromise, and playing a mission teaches that faster than reading about it.
details:
What it does

Mission Control is a browser game in which up to four players plan, build and fly a space mission together. Each player has one job from a real mission team:

  • Planner: splits the budget between the others and settles disputes.
  • Scientist: chooses the objective and the instruments.
  • Designer: builds the spacecraft (power, propulsion, antenna, computer, structure), picks the launch vehicle, and approves what goes on board.
  • Radio Operator: picks the ground stations and talks to the spacecraft in flight.

The team negotiates over money, mass, power, data and time. For example, the Designer can push back on the Scientist's instrument list twice, then take the dispute to the Planner. When everyone is ready, they hold a go/no-go poll and launch.

The game never blocks a bad design. The mission flies as a 3D time-lapse from countdown to arrival, and the design decides how it ends: success, partial success, or one of twelve distinct mission-ending failures. A debrief then explains each problem: what happened, why, whose decision caused it, how to fix it, and a NASA page to learn more. Players can fix the design and fly again.

Benefits and intended impact

The game is for people who love space but have no technical background. It teaches orbits, payload capacity, power budgets, data rates and communications coverage by letting players feel the trade-offs. It also shows that a mission is a team effort where every choice costs someone else something. It runs in a browser with nothing to install, in English and Arabic, so a classroom or a group of friends can play in minutes. It has a guided tutorial, three mission types, three difficulty levels, and solo, shared-device and online play.

Tools and technology

  • TypeScript, React and Vite for the application; Tailwind CSS for styling.
  • three.js (with React Three Fiber) for the 3D planets, spacecraft and flight.
  • Supabase Realtime for online rooms.
  • Vitest and Testing Library, with 427 automated tests covering the game rules and screens.
  • Python for a reference model that checks every mission can be won.
  • Vercel for hosting.
  • NASA resources: planet, Moon and star imagery; the NASA Image and Video Library; Basics of Space Flight; the Earth Observatory orbit catalogue; Deep Space Network pages; and the colours of NASA's Horizon Design System.

How it is creative

Failure is the teacher. Instead of warnings, players see their spacecraft tumble, lose contact or miss Mars, and a parody Flight Director reacts to the result. The lesson comes from the argument between roles, not from a text screen.

What we considered

  • Accuracy against simplicity: the numbers are real public figures, rounded for play, and the game says so.
  • Fair accountability: each failure is traced to the role that made the decision.
  • Access: two languages with right-to-left support, and a mode for one shared device.
  • Respect for NASA's rules: credited NASA images, no NASA logos, and a clear notice that the game is fan-made and not endorsed by NASA.
